pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11 (PROCEDURAL). How palaeontologists work — the full workflow from finding a fossil to publishing what it means — taught by running the process in order and seeing that method (and the right tool) protects the evidence.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 working-scientifically (planning, gathering, recording, presenting; using evidence) applied to Y3 Rocks/fossils and Y6 Evolution.
• Standards — US (NGSS): Science & Engineering Practices (planning investigations, analysing data, constructing explanations, communicating information) built around 3-LS4-1 fossils-as-evidence.
• Operational details: sequence the workflow — (1) PROSPECT; (2) EXCAVATE carefully with the appropriate tool; (3) record context (map, photograph, label — provenance matters); (4) PLASTER-JACKET and transport; (5) PREPARE in the lab; (6) study, compare, PUBLISH/peer-review. Skipping steps or using the wrong tool destroys irreplaceable information.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): put the main steps in order (find → dig → protect → clean → study). Tier B (transitional, ~10): choose the right tool for a delicate bone and say why recording WHERE it was found matters. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain why context and publication/peer review make a find scientific evidence rather than just an old bone.
bestPractices: Have children perform the workflow IN ORDER, so the logic of each step (why record before removing) is experienced, not memorised.
Tie tool choice to consequence — delicate tools for delicate bone — so care is understood as protecting data.
Stress provenance: mapping and photographing position captures information that vanishes once a fossil is lifted.
Include the lab and publication stages so science is seen as continuing past the dig into analysis and peer review.
Use real roles (prospector, preparator, curator) to show palaeontology as collaborative, methodical work rather than lone treasure-hunting.
keyRepresentations: A staged workflow strip: prospect → excavate → record → jacket → prepare → study/publish.
A field tool tray contrasting fine tools (brush, awl) with coarse ones (hammer, pick).
A grid-mapped, photographed dig site showing bones in situ.
A plaster jacket protecting a bone for transport.
A lab prep bench with a fossil being cleaned of matrix under magnification.
commonMisconceptions: 'You just dig fossils out fast' — excavation is slow, careful, and documented; speed destroys evidence.
'Where a fossil was found doesn't matter, only the bone' — context (layer, position, associates) is crucial data.
'Any tool will do' — the wrong tool damages delicate specimens.
'The work ends when the fossil is out of the ground' — preparation, comparison and publication are essential later stages.
'One person makes the discovery alone' — palaeontology is collaborative and peer-reviewed.

learn.summary: Teaches 9–11 year olds the palaeontology workflow as a PROCEDURE run in order — prospect, excavate with the right tool, record context before lifting, plaster-jacket, transport, prepare in the lab, then study, compare and publish. The core insight is that method and tool choice protect irreplaceable evidence: where and how a fossil lay is data lost forever if not recorded before removal, and the right care turns 'an old bone' into scientific evidence. Learners perform the sequence and experience the cost of wrong tools or skipped steps.

activities.title: Lead palaeontologist: run the dig in order
feedback: If a heavy tool is chosen on delicate bone: the bone cracks. Delicate bone needs fine tools (brush, awl). Heavy tools used on or right next to the bone can destroy the specimen and its surrounding detail, though they are used to clear thick rock further away.
If removal is attempted before recording: stop and record first. Once the bone is lifted, its exact position, layer and relationship to nearby specimens can never be fully recovered.
If cleaning is rushed in the lab: fine detail has been lost; preparation must be slow and careful to keep the information the fossil holds.
When the full sequence is followed with care: the specimen keeps maximum evidence value and can be properly described, compared and published.
activities.rationale: Procedures are understood by performing them in order with real consequences, so the logic of each step (why record before removing) is experienced rather than memorised. Tying tool choice to a visible consequence frames care as protecting data. Proposed activity; not yet validated.
sourceClaims: Palaeontology fieldwork follows a disciplined workflow — prospecting, careful excavation with appropriate tools, recording context, plaster-jacketing, transport, lab preparation, study and publication.
Recording a fossil's precise location and context (provenance) is essential; information about position and associated specimens is lost forever if not documented before removal.
learnerActions: Prospect a landscape and choose where to dig — crumbling sedimentary badlands where bones of the right age surface, not granite hills — and say why.
Pick a tool from a tray at a find: try a heavy pick/hammer and observe the fragile bone cracking, then switch to a fine brush and awl and watch the fossil emerge intact.
Before lifting the bone, complete a required recording step — photograph, grid-map and label the bone's position and rock layer in place — and only then proceed to removal.

Once the bone is recorded and exposed on a pedestal of rock, plaster-jacket it in place, then undercut and lift the jacketed block for transport. Next, prepare it in the lab (note that rushing the cleaning strips away fine detail).
Compare the prepared fossil to known skeletons, write a scientific description of it, and submit that description for peer review and publication.
State in one sentence why the same bone can become valuable scientific evidence (and perhaps a museum display) if the method is followed, but just a curio if it isn't.
activities.intendedInsight: Each step exists for a reason: recording position captures data that vanishes once a fossil is lifted, the right tool protects a fragile specimen, and lab preparation, comparison and publication are what make a find into scientific evidence rather than just an old bone.

activities.title: Explore an annotated dig-site scene
feedback: Confirm each zone's purpose when revealed, and name the tool and reason it suits that task.
Prompt: which stage captures information that would otherwise be lost? (recording position and layer in the field).
activities.rationale: An annotated, explorable scene can convey stages, tools and vocabulary clearly. As a scaffold it introduces the map of the process; it does not by itself make the learner experience the cost of a wrong tool or an out-of-order step, so pair it with performing the sequence.
sourceClaims: Palaeontology fieldwork follows a disciplined workflow — prospecting, careful excavation with appropriate tools, recording context, plaster-jacketing, transport, lab preparation, study and publication.
learnerActions: Move through zones of a labelled scene — field dig → plaster jacket → lab prep bench → study/comparison → publication — and reveal at each what happens and which tool is used.
At the field zone, identify which tools are fine (brush, awl) and which are coarse (hammer, pick), and which belong on delicate bone.
At the lab zone, look at a fossil being cleaned of surrounding rock (matrix) under magnification and describe why this stage matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Intended to build the vocabulary and mental map of the full workflow and the tools and purpose of each stage, from field to lab to publication.

activities.title: Check: order and justify the workflow
feedback: If recording is placed after lifting (or left out): position, layer and associated specimens can only be captured while the bone is still in place, so recording must come before removal.

If jacketing is placed before excavation: the jacket goes on only after the bone has been carefully exposed and recorded, while it still sits on a pedestal of rock. It holds the bone together as it is lifted and transported, so it cannot come before excavation or replace it.
If 'study and publish' is placed before lab preparation: the fossil must be cleaned and prepared in the lab before it can be properly described and studied.
If heavy tools or fast digging are chosen first with no risk seen: fossils are fragile and unique — a rushed dig near the bone can shatter the specimen and destroy surrounding evidence.
Full response orders the sequence AND explains why recording, careful excavation and jacketing protect a fragile, irreplaceable fossil.
activities.rationale: Ordering and justifying checks knowledge of the process and surfaces the common sequence errors (recording too late, jacketing before digging, studying before cleaning). Because it asks for justification it elicits reasoning as well as recognition; it still checks understanding rather than performance, so use it alongside the hands-on run.
sourceClaims: Recording a fossil's precise location and context (provenance) is essential; information about position and associated specimens is lost forever if not documented before removal.
learnerActions: Put the workflow stages in order: prospect for exposed fossils → carefully expose the bone with small tools and record its position and rock layer (photograph, grid-map, label) → wrap it in a plaster jacket while it still sits on a pedestal of rock → undercut and lift the jacketed block → transport to the lab → prepare and clean in the lab → study and publish.
Match each tool to its task, and explain why a plaster jacket is used (to hold the fragile fossil and its surrounding rock together while it is lifted out and transported).
Answer why recording exactly where and in which rock layer a fossil was found matters before removal.
Explain what could be lost forever if a fossil is dug out carelessly.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can both sequence the process — including recording context before removal — and justify the care steps, reasoning about what rushing would destroy.

activities.title: Interview a working palaeontologist
feedback: Draw attention to any answer explaining why provenance and careful method matter, and connect it back to the steps the learner has performed.
If the discussion stays general, prompt for a specific step and its reason.
activities.rationale: An authentic interview is engaging and can reinforce the collaborative, peer-reviewed nature of the field. It may explain the procedure and the reasons behind each step, but does not by itself provide structured hands-on practice of executing the sequence, so it complements rather than replaces performing the sequence.
learnerActions: Prepare and ask questions of a field palaeontologist, including: 'What would you never do at a dig site, and why?' and 'Why do you record where a bone was found before lifting it?'
After the discussion, summarise one thing that changed or confirmed your understanding of the workflow.
activities.intendedInsight: Shows palaeontology as collaborative, methodical work — with real roles such as prospector, preparator and curator — rather than lone treasure-hunting.

activities.title: Optional: uncover a bone in a 3D quarry
feedback: If the wrong tool or depth damages the bone: slow down and choose a finer tool — the goal is to expose, not break, the specimen.
Prompt the learner to record the arrangement before lifting.
activities.rationale: A spatial excavation may add embodiment and make in-situ arrangement vivid. The workflow's key decision points — tool choice, documentation, sequence — can also be conveyed in a 2D run, and no comparative evidence establishes the 3D version is more effective, so treat this as optional enrichment rather than a requirement.
learnerActions: At a 3D quarry, choose depth and tool to brush away surrounding rock and reveal a partly buried bone, exposing how it lies in space.
Describe the spatial arrangement of the bone before removing it, and record its position.
activities.intendedInsight: Adds a sense of embodiment to excavation and makes the spatial arrangement of a buried specimen concrete.

constraints: The hands-on run of the sequence is the primary proposed activity for this PROCEDURAL objective; the annotated scene and the ordering check are scaffolds — the scene introduces vocabulary and map but does not enforce order or consequences, and the check confirms knowledge (with justification) rather than physical performance.

Keep provenance central: recording layer, position and associated specimens before removal captures information that cannot be recovered once a fossil is lifted; this recording step appears in both the performed run and the ordering check.
Tie tool choice to consequence (fine tools for fragile bone) so care is understood as protecting data, not an arbitrary rule.

Include the lab and publication stages so science is seen as continuing past the dig into preparation, comparison and publication; a well-documented find is usually kept in a museum research collection, where it may also go on display.
The interview and the 3D quarry are complementary; do not treat them as substitutes for performing the full workflow in order.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row.

All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions; cited claims support the underlying teaching principle but do not establish that these specific activities were tested or are comparatively more effective.

The source assessment's 'correctAnswer' and 'evidence' list omit the explicit record-context step (photograph/grid-map/label) as a distinct stage, though provenance is emphasised throughout; the activities restore recording as its own step before removal in both the hands-on run and the ordering check for consistency with the provenance claim.

The source evidence list ends at 'study, display' while the correctAnswer ends at 'study and publish'; the rewrite keeps publish/peer-review and treats 'display' as the museum-centrepiece outcome — a reconciliation of a minor source inconsistency, not new verification.
Framing publication as peer review mildly extends the source's 'study and publication'; retained as normal field practice rather than independently verified efficacy.
Fit rankings, product/catalog vocabulary and quiz-step identifiers from the source have been removed; alternatives are retained by pedagogical purpose only.

probeDeeper: Why do palaeontologists record exactly where and in which rock layer a fossil was found before removing it?
What could be lost forever if a fossil is dug out carelessly?
Why plaster specifically for the journey, rather than just putting it in a box?
assess.correctAnswer: Prospect for exposed fossils → dig it out carefully with small tools → wrap it in a plaster jacket → transport it to the lab → prepare and clean it in the lab → study and publish. Careful small-tool excavation avoids breaking the fragile fossil and preserves its context; the plaster jacket protects the freed fossil during transport.

errorPatterns.pattern: Just dig it out fast, with big tools like any other digging.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Stress that fossils are fragile and unique; show how a rushed dig shatters the specimen and destroys the surrounding evidence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Skips careful excavation or puts heavy tools first, seeing no risk.

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrap it in plaster before (or instead of) digging it out.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify the jacket protects an already-freed fossil for the journey, so it comes after careful excavation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places jacketing ahead of excavation in the sequence.

errorPatterns.pattern: Study or display the fossil before it's prepared and cleaned.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note the fossil must be cleaned and prepared in the lab before it can be properly described and studied.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders 'study and publish' before lab preparation.

responseLevels.gap: Jumbles the sequence and sees no reason for care, treating it like ordinary digging.
responseLevels.full: Orders the full workflow correctly AND explains why careful excavation and plaster jacketing protect a fragile, irreplaceable fossil, reasoning about what rushing would destroy.
responseLevels.partial: Gets most of the order right but can't justify the careful-excavation or jacketing steps, or misplaces one stage.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A palaeontologist has just spotted a dinosaur bone poking out of a hillside. Put these jobs in the order she'd actually do them, and as you go explain WHY each step is done: study and publish; wrap it in a plaster jacket; dig it out carefully with small tools; transport it to the lab; prepare and clean it in the lab; prospect for exposed fossils. If any step would be risky to rush, say what would go wrong.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the workflow sequences it and justifies careful digging and jacketing. A child who doesn't jumbles the order (jacketing before digging, studying before cleaning) or can't say why care is needed.
